jhmt-2020-tr1-01.title: Equality as a set of pairs
jhmt-2020-tr1-01.body: Yes. Equality on $\mathbb R$ is the set of ordered pairs $R=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb R\}$ with ground set $\mathbb R$: we have $x=y$ exactly when $(x,y)\in R$. A relation is just a set of ordered pairs of elements of the ground set, so equality is a relation.

jhmt-2020-tr1-02.title: Comparability fails
jhmt-2020-tr1-02.body: No. Conditions 1–3 do hold ($a\mid a$; if $a\mid b$ and $b\mid a$ for positive $a,b$ then $a=b$; divisibility is transitive), but condition 4 fails: $5$ does not divide $7$ and $7$ does not divide $5$, so neither $(5,7)$ nor $(7,5)$ is in $R$.

jhmt-2020-tr1-03.title: Check the three conditions
jhmt-2020-tr1-03.body:
Here $T\subset S$ means every element of $T$ is an element of $S$.

1. **Reflexive.** Every element of $A_i$ is an element of $A_i$, so $A_i\subset A_i$.
2. **Antisymmetric.** Let $A_i\ne A_j$ with $A_i\subset A_j$. Since the sets differ and every element of $A_i$ lies in $A_j$, some element of $A_j$ is not in $A_i$. Hence $A_j\not\subset A_i$.
3. **Transitive.** Suppose $A_i\subset A_j$ and $A_j\subset A_k$. If $x\in A_i$, then $x\in A_j$, and therefore $x\in A_k$. So $A_i\subset A_k$.

So the subset relation is a partial order.

jhmt-2020-tr1-04.title: Check the three conditions
jhmt-2020-tr1-04.body:
1. **Reflexive.** For every $a$, $a\le a$, so $a\le_c a$.
2. **Antisymmetric.** Let $a\ne b$ with $b\le_c a$, i.e. $a\le b$. By antisymmetry of $\le$, $b\not\le a$, which means $a\not\le_c b$.
3. **Transitive.** Suppose $c\le_c b$ and $b\le_c a$. Then $b\le c$ and $a\le b$, so $a\le b\le c$ and by transitivity of $\le$, $a\le c$. That is, $c\le_c a$.

So $\le_c$ is a partial order on $A$.

jhmt-2020-tr1-05.title: Coordinatewise order
jhmt-2020-tr1-05.body:
One example: $(x_1,x_2)\le(y_1,y_2)$ if and only if $x_1\le y_1$ and $x_2\le y_2$.

This is a partial order. It is reflexive. It is antisymmetric, because $x_1\le y_1\le x_1$ and $x_2\le y_2\le x_2$ force the two points to be equal. It is transitive, because each coordinate is. It is not total: $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are incomparable. The lexicographic order ($x_1<y_1$, or $x_1=y_1$ and $x_2\le y_2$) is another valid example, and it is even total.

Ordering points by their distance from the origin does **not** work: distinct points such as $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ would each be $\le$ the other, which violates antisymmetry.

jhmt-2020-tr1-06.title: Antisymmetry
jhmt-2020-tr1-06.body: Suppose $g$ and $g'$ are distinct greatest elements. Since $g$ is greatest and $g'\ne g$, we get $g'<g$, so $g'\le g$. Since $g'$ is greatest, likewise $g\le g'$. But $g\ne g'$, so by antisymmetry $g'\le g$ and $g\le g'$ cannot both hold, a contradiction. Hence a poset has at most one greatest element.

jhmt-2020-tr1-07.title: An antichain
jhmt-2020-tr1-07.body: Let $n\ge2$ and $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$ with $R=\{(s_i,s_i):1\le i\le n\}$, so $s_i\le s_j$ only when $i=j$. This relation is reflexive, and antisymmetry and transitivity hold trivially, since there are no pairs of distinct elements. Any element $g=s_i$ has some other element $s_j\ne g$, and $s_j<g$ fails. So no element is greatest. (For example, two elements that are not compared already work. For $n=1$ the single element is trivially greatest, so the claim is about general $n$.)

jhmt-2020-tr1-08.title: Build an increasing chain
jhmt-2020-tr1-08.body:
Let the poset have $n\ge1$ elements and suppose no element is maximal. Pick any $x_1$. Since $x_1$ is not maximal there is $x_2$ with $x_1<x_2$; since $x_2$ is not maximal there is $x_3$ with $x_2<x_3$, and so on. This gives $x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_{n+1}$.

**These are distinct.** By transitivity, $x_i\le x_j$ whenever $i\le j$. If $x_i=x_j$ for some $i<j$, then $x_{i+1}\le x_j=x_i$ and also $x_i\le x_{i+1}$ with $x_i\ne x_{i+1}$, contradicting antisymmetry.

So the poset has at least $n+1$ distinct elements, a contradiction. Hence some element is maximal.

jhmt-2020-tr1-09.title: Upper bound and construction
jhmt-2020-tr1-09.body:
Let $n\ge2$ (for $n=1$ every partial order is total).

**Upper bound.** A partial order contains the $n$ pairs $(a,a)$. For each of the $\binom n2$ unordered pairs $\{a,b\}$ of distinct elements, antisymmetry allows at most one of $(a,b),(b,a)$. A partial order that is not total has at least one pair $\{a,b\}$ with neither, so it has at most $n+\binom n2-1$ ordered pairs.

**Construction.** Take a total order $s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_n$, which has $n+\binom n2$ pairs, and remove the single pair $(s_1,s_2)$. The result is still reflexive and antisymmetric. It is still transitive: a violation would need $(s_1,c)$ and $(c,s_2)$ in the relation with $c\ne s_1,s_2$, i.e. $s_1<c<s_2$, and no such $c$ exists. It is not total, since $s_1$ and $s_2$ are incomparable. It has $\binom n2+n-1$ pairs.

So the maximum is $\binom{n}{2}+n-1$.

jhmt-2020-tr1-10.title: Sizes strictly increase along a chain
jhmt-2020-tr1-10.body:
**At most $n+1$.** List the elements of a chain as $C_1\subset C_2\subset\cdots\subset C_k$; any two are comparable, so they can be ordered this way. If $C_i\subset C_{i+1}$ and $C_i\ne C_{i+1}$, then $C_{i+1}$ has an element not in $C_i$, so $|C_i|<|C_{i+1}|$. Thus the sizes $|C_1|<\cdots<|C_k|$ are distinct integers in $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$, and $k\le n+1$.

**Exactly $n+1$.** Writing $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$, the chain $\varnothing\subset\{s_1\}\subset\{s_1,s_2\}\subset\cdots\subset S$, built by adding one element at a time, has $n+1$ elements.

So the height is $n+1$.

jhmt-2020-tr1-11.title: LYM inequality
jhmt-2020-tr1-11.body:
Let $\mathcal F$ be an antichain of subsets of $S$. A *maximal chain* $\varnothing\subset\{x_1\}\subset\{x_1,x_2\}\subset\cdots\subset S$ corresponds to an ordering $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $S$, so there are $n!$ of them. A set $A$ with $|A|=k$ lies on exactly $k!(n-k)!$ maximal chains, and a maximal chain contains at most one member of the antichain $\mathcal F$. Hence
$$\sum_{A\in\mathcal F}|A|!\,(n-|A|)!\le n!\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_{A\in\mathcal F}\frac{1}{\binom{n}{|A|}}\le1.$$
Since $\binom nk\le\binom n{n/2}$ for all $k$, this gives $|\mathcal F|\le\binom{n}{n/2}$. The family of all $\frac n2$-element subsets is an antichain of that size (two different sets of the same size are never nested), so $w=\binom n{n/2}$.

If $|\mathcal F|=w$, then $1\ge\sum_{A\in\mathcal F}\binom n{|A|}^{-1}\ge\frac{|\mathcal F|}{\binom n{n/2}}=1$, so equality holds termwise: $\binom n{|A|}=\binom n{n/2}$ for every $A\in\mathcal F$. For even $n$ the middle binomial coefficient is strictly larger than all others, so every $A\in\mathcal F$ has exactly $\frac n2$ elements. Then $\mathcal F$ is a subfamily of the $\frac n2$-element subsets of the same size, so it is all of them.

So exactly $\boxed{1}$ antichain has size $w$.

jhmt-2020-tr1-12.title: Layer by longest chain ending at each element
jhmt-2020-tr1-12.body:
(Here $S$ is finite.) For $s\in S$ let $x_s$ be the largest number of elements in a chain whose greatest element is $s$. Since $\{s\}$ is such a chain and every chain has at most $h$ elements, $1\le x_s\le h$. Let $A_i=\{s\in S:x_s=i\}$ for $i=1,\dots,h$. Every element lies in exactly one $A_i$.

**Each $A_i$ is an antichain.** Suppose $s,t\in A_i$ are distinct and comparable, say $s<t$. Take a chain $C$ with $x_s$ elements and greatest element $s$. Every $c\in C$ satisfies $c\le s<t$, so $C\cup\{t\}$ is a chain with greatest element $t$ and $x_s+1$ elements (as $t\notin C$, since $t\le s$ would contradict antisymmetry). So $x_t\ge x_s+1$, contradicting $x_s=x_t=i$.

**Each $A_i$ is nonempty.** Take a chain $c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_h$ with $h$ elements. The chain $\{c_1,\dots,c_i\}$ shows $x_{c_i}\ge i$. If $x_{c_i}>i$, a chain with more than $i$ elements ending at $c_i$, together with $c_{i+1},\dots,c_h$, would be a chain with more than $h$ elements. So $x_{c_i}=i$ and $c_i\in A_i$.

Thus $A_1,\dots,A_h$ is a partition of $S$ into $h$ antichains.

jhmt-2020-tr1-13.title: Partition and pigeonhole
jhmt-2020-tr1-13.body: Let $h$ be the height, so $1\le h\le m$. By Problem 12 the ground set splits into $h$ antichains $A_1,\dots,A_h$. If every $A_i$ had at most $n$ elements, the poset would have at most $hn\le mn<mn+1$ elements, a contradiction. So some antichain has at least $n+1$ elements, and the width is at least $n+1$.
